d_finding1_committed_switch_topology_doe._claim: The COMMITTED receiving-side-only transfer switch does not compose into a chain. With the cut only on the receiving side, the SOURCE bank stays permanently wired to its own outgoing inductor, so while bank N is being CHARGED its outgoing inductor is a shunt resonator hanging off it.
d_finding1_committed_switch_topology_doe._isolation: a277_rxonly and a277_free differ ONLY by the presence of the source-side cut. Same cells, same banks, same head gate, same L, same switch widths, same phases.

consequences_MEASURED.note: tau = 2L/R = 55.6 ns, so the ring CANNOT damp inside any usable inter-hop gap: hop 2 can never start from rest.

cost_of_the_fix_MEASURED.why: a chainable bank carries TWO transfer-switch terminals (one incoming, one outgoing) where the committed single-hop destination carried one, and the tg15p switch is 15 um of device width against a bank of 14.9 um of cell width. Source-cut conduction loss is negligible (I^2R 0.137 fJ of a 23.8 fJ hop).

d_finding1_committed_switch_topology_doe._secondary: Holding the committed destination park ON while a hop is idle is UNSAFE with a receiving-side-only cut (it shorts the source rail to ground through the inductor -- the committed AMENDMENT-A3 failure) but becomes SAFE and NECESSARY once the source side is cut: it is what pins the otherwise-floating inductor island. MEASURED: leaving that island floating aborts the run at the first gate edge.

e_validation_at_the_known_good_slow_poin.why_minus_0p56_pct_per_hop_cannot_apply: The recorded -0.56%/hop (qal_a1f_chain.py, qal_a1f_chain_bare.cir) was MEASURED on an IDEAL LC chain: 6 LINEAR 10 fF capacitors, BEHAVIOURAL VSWITCH switches with RON = 1 ohm, L = 1 uH, R = 100 ohm, Q ~ 141, dV = 0.6, total loss 0.097 fJ over 5 hops. There are NO DEVICES and NO GATES in that deck at all. It is an I^2R-only number. The real device hop's MEASURED loss is 8.383 fJ out of ~18 fJ stored, of which ~6.65 fJ is switch-related and only 0.050 fJ is I^2R -- so the term -0.56%/hop describes is 0.6% of the real per-hop loss. The COMMITTED SINGLE HOP ITSELF already droops -32.4% (1.000 V source -> 0.6759 V delivered); no chain built from it could ever have shown -0.56%/hop.

measured_per_hop_droop.steady_state_estimate_is_hop2: hop 2 is the representative hop: both of its ends are real gate banks at realistic levels, whereas hop 1's source starts at the saturated top of the bank's Q-V curve.

measured_per_hop_droop.direction_of_the_residual_bias: hop 2's droop is an OPTIMISTIC (under-) estimate of steady state: rail 3 carries only an incoming switch terminal, with no outgoing one, so it is lighter than a mid-pipeline bank would be.
measured_per_hop_droop.mechanism: per-hop fixed CHARGE absorbed by the transfer switch against the bank's incremental capacitance. MEASURED at the anchor: 62.15 fC flowed through L1 while the destination bank's own static charge at its delivered rail is only ~23 fC; the bank's measured incremental capacitance at the operating point is 36.6 fF, so the absorbed charge IS the rail droop. It is a switch-charge/bank-capacitance ratio, not an I^2R effect, so it does not improve with Q.

MEASURED_device_asymmetry_that_makes_it_._note: the single-hop deck held pull-down gates at 1.000 V, ABOVE the 0.676 V rail those cells run on -- non-physical, and worth 7.7x in drive.

THE_DEEPER_MECHANISM_measured._statement: The chain's pull-down failure is NOT just reduced overdrive. It is that the predecessor's logic HIGH is referenced to the predecessor's RAIL, and that rail is being drained forward by the very hop that powers the successor. A logic LOW is referenced to GROUND and survives intact; a logic HIGH does not. So the device driven by a HIGH -- the nMOS pull-down -- loses its gate drive DURING its own evaluation window, and there is no buffer to hold it.
THE_DEEPER_MECHANISM_measured.why_a_shorter_hop_helps_a_little: the collapse is slower in absolute terms at small L only because the whole hop is shorter; the HIGH still falls 34-62% before the hop reaches its own current zero.
THE_DEEPER_MECHANISM_measured.second_order_compounding: the HIGH level degrades STAGE OVER STAGE independently of the rail: bank 2's pull-downs are driven at 0.977 V (from bank 1, an ideal-source chain head at dV), bank 3's at only 0.620-0.690 V (from bank 2, a real bank). That is why bank 3 is worse than bank 2 at every single L and every stagger, and why a 4th stage would be worse again.

CAUSAL_CONTROL_h277_hold._design: identical deck, identical L (277.8 nH), identical switch, identical cells, identical top-up, identical 300 ps stage time, identical bank-2 rail (0.70141 V to five digits). The ONLY difference: hop 2 never closes, so bank 2's charge is NOT transferred forward and its HIGH outputs are not drained.

bank3_pulldown_data_pattern_guard.transferred: FAIL (output 0.238 x rail, gate is <= 0.10 x rail)

CAUSAL_CONTROL_h277_hold.CONCLUSION: The pull-down failure is caused SPECIFICALLY by the forward charge transfer collapsing the predecessor's HIGH level. It is not rail droop, not the switch, not L, not the stage time, and not the cells: hold the predecessor up and the same cell on the same rail goes from 76.23% to 100.14% and lands its output at ground. This is a STRUCTURAL property of an unbuffered forward-transfer chain, not a parametric one, which is exactly why no L and no stagger fixes it.
CAUSAL_CONTROL_h277_hold._the_control_also_confirms_the_other_lim: in the hold control bank 3's pull-UP becomes the laggard instead (65.3% at the boundary, 82.7% even after the tail), because there bank 3's rail is supplied only by a 20 ps top-up packet and sags to 0.690 V, leaving the pull-up 0.25 V of overdrive. So the two limits are independent and both real: pull-DOWN limited by HIGH-level collapse, pull-UP limited by rail level.

i_TOPUP_COST._metric: E = dV * dQ on the always-connected ideal dV source, dQ from a 1F integrator t0-referenced at 0.5 ps and split by DISJOINT checkpoint windows (head, bank-2 window, bank-3 window). Exact, because the supply is a constant-voltage source. MEASURED.
i_TOPUP_COST._reference_for_comparison: the committed single hop's own dissipation E_hop_open = 8.3828 fJ.
i_TOPUP_COST.HEADLINE_COST: 15.2 to 29.1 fJ of delivered energy per bank per hop (L = 277.8 nH down to 3 nH), against the committed single hop's own 8.383 fJ of dissipation. The top-up therefore costs 1.8x to 3.5x the loss it repairs.
i_TOPUP_COST.why_it_is_so_expensive: it is a RESISTIVE transfer from a fixed dV source into a bank, so it is not adiabatic; and the top-up window overlaps the cells' own settling, so the supply ends up delivering the cells' switching charge as well as the transfer deficit. Subtracting the measured static stored energy of the 8-cell bank bounds the dissipated part at 10.1-23.1 fJ per bank per hop.
i_TOPUP_COST.the_unavoidable_tension_MEASURED: a SHORT top-up window (restore only) leaves the rail to sag as the cells draw from it -- 0.792 V with a 15 ps window at DELTA = 27 ps, falling to 0.701 V with a 20 ps window and a 300 ps gap, because the bank pays for its own gates out of its own rail. A LONG window clamps the rail to the supply and the top-up then simply IS the power supply, at which point the resonant transfer is decoration. This tension, not the droop arithmetic, is what 'top-up -> lossless-in-level' has to answer.

j_HEADLINE.pre_registered_acceptance: every gate in ALL THREE banks >= 90% settling at its own stage boundary AND the chain inside the 120 mV margin budget.
j_HEADLINE.ANSWER: THERE IS NO SUCH L. Not free-running, not topped up, at no inductance from 277.8 nH down to 3 nH (a 93x range) and no stagger from 27 to 300 ps. 23 measured chain rows, zero pass.

single_hop_comparator_frozen_from_the_co.settling: all 8 cells 100% at the settle checkpoint

THE_NUMBER_A_THROUGHPUT_CLAIM_HAS_TO_USE._and_the_caveat_that_travels_with_it: that 2.10x is measured at a 75% settling threshold the single hop meets at 100%. At the pre-registered 90% the chain has no operating point at all, so 2.10x is a FLOOR on the penalty, not the penalty.

also_the_hop_itself_got_slower.why: a chainable bank carries TWO transfer-switch terminals (incoming and outgoing) where the committed single-hop destination carried one. The source-side cut is not optional -- without it 42.3% of the hop's charge leaks into the idle next-stage inductor.

j_HEADLINE.so_is_the_hop_time_the_stage_time: The architecture point is right in the sense that matters: there is no flop, latch or buffer between levels, so there is no clock-to-Q, no setup and no skew per stage. But the stage time is NOT the hop time. MEASURED, the stage time is t_zcs + a settling allowance, and the allowance is the larger term: at L = 10 nH the hop is 71.2 ps and the chain still had not settled at DELTA = 300 ps. Removing the register did not make the stage time equal to the transfer time; it made the stage time equal to the CELL time, and the cell time is set by the rail level and the input drive, both of which the transfer itself degrades.
j_HEADLINE.L_is_not_the_knob: bank 3's worst pull-down settling varies 72.1-77.6% over a 93x range in L, and 65.1-75.3% over a 2.5x range in stage time at fixed L, asymptoting below 90% in both. The binding constraint is structural (the HIGH level collapses as the predecessor's rail is drained forward), so it does not have an L at which it goes away.

k_what_would_have_to_change.1_hold_the_predecessor: the causal control proves this works (76.23% -> 100.14%), but holding bank N up means NOT transferring its charge forward, which is the energy argument.
k_what_would_have_to_change.2_buffer_or_keep_the_level: a latch/keeper on each output holds the HIGH through the transfer -- and reintroduces exactly the per-stage register the throughput case was built on removing.
k_what_would_have_to_change.3_differential_dual_rail: a differential pair carries the data in the DIFFERENCE, so a common-mode rail collapse does not destroy it. The campaign record already notes dual-rail is needed for the POWER DELIVERY (data-independent per-bank charge); this run says the LOGIC may need it too, which the record explicitly concluded it did not ('dual-rail OPTIONAL not required for completeness').
k_what_would_have_to_change.4_power_the_successor_from_elsewhere: if bank N+1's rail came up from its own top-up while bank N was still up, and bank N were drained afterwards, the collapse would not overlap the evaluation. That is a different architecture (the recycle would have to go somewhere other than the immediate successor) and is not measured here.
k_what_would_have_to_change._what_does_NOT_help_MEASURED: smaller L (flat), longer stage time (asymptotes), the switch widths at the levels tested, or the rail top-up by itself (it fixes the rail, not the input HIGH).

l_negative_results_and_honesty.what_could_still_be_wrong: the settling criterion is a RATIO to the instantaneous rail, inherited from the committed campaign. It is the right criterion for a pull-up but it flatters nothing for a pull-down: a pull-down reading 76% has its output at 0.238 x its rail, and the independent data-pattern guard (pull-down <= 0.10 x rail) fails on exactly those gates and passes in the hold control. Two independent criteria agree, so the conclusion does not rest on the ratio convention.
